task: Write one sentence of your own using the word inane. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know inane should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The seminar's message board drowned in inane replies — "so true!!" and rows of clapping hands — until the professor required a question in every post.
A pointless meeting can be full of perfectly intelligent sentences that lead nowhere; inane talk is empty of sense as well as purpose.
Nonsensical goes past inane — inane chatter is vacant but parseable; nonsense can't even be unscrambled.

Vapid talk is flat and lifeless — nothing sparkles, nothing surprises, the flavor has boiled away. Inane is the harder charge: not merely dull but silly, a remark with no meaning in it at all. A vapid speech still says something, tediously; inane chatter only fills air.

Mindless points at the process: something done or said on autopilot, with no thought behind it. Inane judges the product instead — the remark itself is silly and meaningless, however much or little thinking produced it. A mindless routine can still yield sense; an inane one has none to give.

Latin inanis built no other common English word — inane and its noun inanity are the whole family. Writers once tried "the inane" as a noun for empty space itself; it never caught on.
Inane means silly and meaningless.
Forty floors of elevator rides taught Renata the anatomy of inane conversation.

"Mondays, huh?" "Cold enough for you?" "Working hard or hardly working?" In nine years, she reckoned, she had spent two full days trading words that carried no information, no opinion, and no risk — syllables shaped like talk, performing talk's motions, saying nothing.
Inane is the exact word because the chatter is silly and meaningless — empty the way the Latin root inanis promises: a void with sound in it.
The word doesn't accuse anyone of malice or stupidity; elevators demand noise.
But when a remark could be swapped for a cough with no loss of content, inane has found its specimen.
Inane is for remarks, questions, and pastimes that are empty — silly and meaningless without necessarily being smug about it.
When the speaker is also congratulating himself, reach for this unit's fatuous; when the fault is treating a complex thing as simple, that's simplistic.
Inane is the lightest of the three: a vacancy, not a vice.

The suggestion box was Principal Vo's idea, and for the first month it looked like a triumph: forty slips a week.
But when the student council typed them up, most were inane — 'make school more fun!!', 'less boring classes', a drawing of a shark.
The slips weren't rude, and they weren't off-topic.
They simply carried no meaning a planner could act on: silliness in the shape of suggestions.
Council members sorted the pile twice, hunting for sense, and kept eleven slips out of one hundred sixty.
Vo posted the eleven by the office door — proof, she said, that the box worked, just more rarely than hoped.
